subject: Latency SLO tiers and uptime anchoring proposal
messages:
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.inference.com>

Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.inference.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.inference.com>

Subject: Latency SLO tiers and uptime anchoring proposal

Hi Sam —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Based on our call I pulled together a compact proposal for how Redwood can represent both uptime commitments and latency SLOs in a single template without adding negotiation overhead for routine purchases. The goal is to make the "anchor" for uptime and the latency bands explicit so procurement/legal can quickly map to your internal risk buckets.

Key points in the attached: 
- Standard uptime anchor: 99.95% monthly availability (applies to hosted API endpoints by region).
- Latency SLO tiers (observed at the route level): p50 <= 40ms, p95 <= 180ms, p99 <= 350ms.
- Credit schedule (monthly):
  * Availability >= 99.95%: no credit
  * 99.9% <= Availability < 99.95%: 5% of monthly bill (per service area)
  * 99.0% <= Availability < 99.9%: 15% of monthly bill
  * Availability < 99.0%: 30% of monthly bill, escalates to negotiated remediation plan
- Latency failures (if p99 exceeds band for the month): 2% credit per impacted route, capped at 10% of monthly bill.

Exceptions & carve-outs we propose (see attached spreadsheet):
- Scheduled maintenance windows: advance notice 72 hours; maintenance windows aligned to region off-peak; maintenance excluded from availability by default.
- Batch/ETL workloads: allowance for elevated p99 during predefined daily batch windows (client can opt-in to categorize specific routes as "batch" to avoid latency credits).
- Canary/rollout impacts: first 24 hours of a model rollout are considered a rollout window and are excluded from uptime credit calculations if the rollout was mutually scheduled.

Attachments: [Attachment: SLA_template_v3.pdf (PDF, 128 KB)], [Attachment: latency-bands-spreadsheet.xlsx (XLSX, 42 KB)]

Next steps I recommend: you and your legal team review the anchor + bandwidth, tell us which routes you want marked as batch, and we’ll draft a redline highlighting the batch carve-out and monthly cap.

Would appreciate confirmation if the 99.95% anchor and the latency band approach are acceptable in principle.

Thanks,

Irene —

Appreciate the clear write-up. A couple quick clarifications from procurement and ops:

1) Batch windows: we run heavy nightly ETL from 01:00–04:00 PT that drives most of our embedding workloads. If we mark those routes as "batch" and accept higher p99 there, will that change the monthly availability calculation? Specifically, we need assurance batch traffic doesn’t create a lower effective availability baseline for customer-facing routes.

2) Monthly cap: what's typical for the cap on credits? Finance will not accept an open-ended credit exposure.

3) Latency credits: fine in principle, but we need the measurement methodology (edge region selection, sampling cadence) spelled out so we can validate any credit triggers.

From an appetite perspective, AstraTech is comfortable with a 99.95% baseline for customer-facing routes but wants the batch carve-out handled such that it cannot dilute uptime for non-batch routes.

Subject: Re: Latency SLO tiers and uptime anchoring proposal

Folks —

Looping legal and finance thinking into this thread. High level responses:

- Measurement: we propose using the synthetic route-level probes that feed our Console metrics (region-specific) with a 1-minute sampling cadence. Payment of credits will be triggered based on monthly aggregated telemetry we host; we are happy to share the telemetry export and the query used to compute p95/p99 so AstraTech can audit.

- Batch carve-out: operationally reasonable. We will require the client to declare which routes are batch at contract signature and provide a time window for each route (we can allow up to two daily windows). Batch-marked routes will be excluded from latency credit calculations and will not be allowed to reduce the availability calculation for non-batch routes.

- Monthly cap: finance recommends a standard cap at 15% of the monthly invoice or USD 50,000 (whichever is lower) for starter customers; enterprise customers can negotiate higher caps tied to committed spend. This is to limit exposure while we ramp.

- Credit stacking: latency credits and availability credits are not stacked. If the same route triggers both, availability credit takes precedence; latency credit will be zeroed for that route for the calculation month.

- Maintenance carve: 72 hours notice and pre-scheduled windows; emergency maintenance requires incident report and retroactive scheduling for credit eligibility.

Irene — if we adopt the above, I recommend we add a short annex to the SLA describing: telemetry query, batch declaration clause, monthly cap clause, and a consolidation example (illustrative numbers) so AstraTech can see how credits would be applied on a sample bill.

Laura Bennett
